In the mid 1960s India began planting high-yield wheat varieties bred in Mexico, along with fertiliser and irrigation. Within about a decade, wheat harvests had roughly doubled and India no longer depended on food imports. It was the start of the Green Revolution in India.

The seeds came from the work of the American plant scientist Norman Borlaug in Mexico. He had bred short, sturdy "semi-dwarf" wheats that resisted disease and did not fall over when heavily fertilised. Given water and fertiliser, they could yield several times more grain than traditional types. In 1965 and 1966 India and Pakistan imported thousands of tonnes of this seed.

The need was urgent. In the mid 1960s India suffered droughts and depended on grain shipments from the United States. Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and his farm minister backed the new wheat, and the Indian scientist M. S. Swaminathan led the effort to adapt and spread it. It took hold first in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, where canal irrigation already existed (see Punjab canal colonies). Rice followed.

India had known terrible famines under colonial rule, the last being the Bengal famine of 1943. Since independence, it has had no famine of that kind. Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.

The gains came with costs: heavy use of water has drained groundwater in Punjab, chemicals have harmed soils and health, and richer farmers with irrigation gained more than poorer ones.
